newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. wants to boost humanitarian demining drive.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants to boost humanitarian demining drive.

text.p: The United States wants to give more help to third-world countries trying to remove anti-personnel landmines, and is encouraging them to set up action centres to coordinate the aid.

"Our policy is to work with the international community to assist countries with a land mine problem, helping them to develop the capability to rid themselves of mines," James Dale Sampson, head of the U.S. Defence Department's Humanitarian Demining Program for Europe and Africa, told Reuters on Friday.
Sampson was the keynote speaker at a seminar on Thursday and Friday entitled "U.S. technology and humanitarian demining" organised by U.S. magazines Defense Week and White House Weekly.
The demining seminar came ahead of a diplomatic conference in Brussels next week which will try to prepare a treaty for a global ban on mines.
The U.S. Defence Department will spend $20 million on demining operations this year, not including the salaries of its troops, and has asked for the budget to be increased to $25 million next year.

U.S. troops themselves do not carry out demining operations but train people in host countries to clear land mines. It has helped set up demining operations in Cambodia, Laos, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Rwanda, Namibia, Mozambique, Honduras, Costa Rica and Nicaragua, while assessment mission are under way in Yemen and Angola.
"It makes no difference whether the U.S. has had an adverserial relationship with the country, it is purely a humanitarian action," Sampson said.
Military or commercial demining is not covered by the programme.

As assistance with humanitarian demining is offered by several national governments, the United Nations, non- governmental organisations (NGOs) and private firms, the U.S. encourages countries to set up structures to coordinate the aid.

"Every country with a mine problem should set up a mine action centre," said Dennis Barlow, director of the James Madison University (JMU) Humanitarian Demining Centre in Harrisonburg, Virginia, told Reuters. The centre is sponsored by the Defence Department.
Barlow said that mine action centres could coordinate the use of equipment and different demining approaches.

The U.S., for instance, insists that all mines are blown up at the place where they are discovered, in order to prevent them being used elsewhere. Many NGO's gather mines in one place and then blow them up collectively.
Mines are among the cheapest weapons to make, but once they are laid, finding and destroying them is a labour-intensive, expensive and dangerous exercise.

There are some 110 million mines in the ground in 68 countries, killing about 26,000 people per year, the seminar organisers said. Experts have estimated the average cost of removing each mine is about $1,000.

Metal detectors and probes are no longer the only tools for clearing mines. Experts at the seminar presented a range of high-tech devices, from autonomous robots and supersonic air blasts to chemical sensing and ground-penetrating radar.
Meanwhile, new mines are being laid at a rate of 20 for every one cleared, the seminar organisers said.
Diplomatic efforts to get a ban on land mines have so far have been unsuccesful.

Next week's Brussels Conference on a Global Ban on Antipersonnel Mines, part of a series of talks started in Ottawa, Canada last year, hopes to get at least 45 states to sign a treaty for a total ban on mines by the end of this year.
The U.S. is not expected to sign that treaty, although it will send observers to the conference. China and Russia, the main producers and users of mines, are ignoring it altogether.

Separately, a U.N.-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva is also trying to start talks about a global ban on arms, but progress there is even slower because of political bickering between the participating nations.
